title: Access, inequality, and the first stage
dek: Why formal access to infrastructure, emergency services, or an instrument does not imply equal effects.
trend: This issue’s common thread is that access is not the same as equal benefit. Broadband reaches rural provinces but initially widens income gaps where complementary skills and institutions are weak. Ambulances formally cover rural Connecticut, yet travel, stationing, and staffing leave response times roughly twice as long. And an instrument can shift treatment while identifying very different returns across people. Across all three, the average effect hides who actually receives the service, how intensely, and with what capacity to convert it into an outcome.

articles.summary: Using all Italian provinces from 2014–2022, the authors apply a continuous-treatment difference-in-differences design to rural broadband rollout. Expansion raises several inequality measures on average, especially in Southern and marginalized provinces; northern areas appear more likely to benefit after coverage reaches a critical mass. The result warns that infrastructure access alone need not equalize outcomes when complementary skills and institutions are unevenly distributed.

paper.title: Digital divide and income inequality: causal evidence from Italian provinces
paper.authors: Angela Stefania Bergantino; Giulio Fusco; Mario Intini; Gianluca Monturano
paper.abstract: Abstract The digital economy can function either as a catalyst to stimulate economic growth or else as a driver of socioeconomic inequality when its benefits are unevenly distributed. This study investigates the effect of rural digital connectivity on income inequality in Italy. Utilizing NUTS 3 panel data spanning 2014–2022, we conduct a counterfactual Difference-in-Differences approach with continuous treatment intensity to estimate the impact of introducing rural broadband coverage at speeds of 30 and 100 Mbps on multiple measures of income distribution, including the Gini, Theil, and Atkinson indices. The empirical framework incorporates a comprehensive set of socioeconomic controls, as well as provincial and time fixed effects, to account for unobserved heterogeneity and regional path dependencies. Our findings indicate that broadband expansion is significantly associated with increasing inequality, suggesting that access alone does not guarantee inclusive outcomes, particularly in localities characterized by structural fragility and limited human capital. Additional heterogeneity and spatial analyses demonstrate that these inequality effects are more evident in southern provinces and localities with a higher concentration of inner areas, where the digital divide remains more pronounced. These findings accentuate the dual role of digitalization and highlight the necessity of coordinated policy interventions that combine infrastructure investment with digital skills development, institutional capacity-building, and spatially integrated governance strategies.

articles.summary: Town-level Connecticut data show rural mean EMS response time near 13 minutes—roughly twice the non-rural mean—while median household income does not explain variation within either group. Geography, stationing, staffing, and volunteer-service capacity look more plausible than town income alone. The evidence is descriptive rather than causal and uses 2016 data.

paper.title: Socioeconomic factors influencing rural-urban ambulance response time disparities in Connecticut
paper.abstract: Abstract Across the U.S, it is a documented fact that rural areas have longer ambulance response times and tend to have lower median income. The objective of this study was to test if the rural-urban emergency medical service (EMS) response time disparity was related to wealth disparity in the state of Connecticut. All mean EMS response times were sourced from the 2016 Office of Emergency Medical Services Data Report. Rural definitions were sourced from the Connecticut Office of Rural Health. Median income data was drawn from the Connecticut Office of Policy and Management. A Mann-Whitney U test determined if the average rural EMS response time was greater than the non-rural EMS response time. Pearson coefficients quantified the relationship between median income and EMS response time. A t-test ascertained if the average median income differed between the two datasets. The mean EMS response time was 12.98 min (SD = 3.36) rural and 8.26 min (SD = 2.12) non-rural. Rural mean response time and median income were not significantly correlated ( r = -.148, p =.247); non-rural mean response time and median income were also not significantly related. No significant disparity was detected (t=0.478, p =.633) between the mean rural household income ($98,258) and mean non-rural household income ($95,706). Significant disparities in EMS response times can exist between rural and non-rural towns separate from median income trends, as is the case in Connecticut. These findings may have limited generalizability because of Connecticut’s relatively high median income as compared to other states yet may be relevant to states with similar economic metrics.

articles.summary: The correlated-random-coefficients estimator combines a conditional-rank control function with local linear regressions to recover average partial effects when treatment effects vary across people. In a returns-to-schooling application, conventional IV implies roughly a 13% wage return per year of schooling while the heterogeneous-effect estimate is nearer 8%. The method still requires valid instruments and defensible control-function assumptions.

paper.title: ivcrc: An Instrumental Variables Estimator for the Correlated Random Coefficients Model
paper.authors: David Benson; Matthew A. Masten; Alexander Torgovitsky
paper.abstract: We discuss the ivcrc module, which implements an instrumental variables (IV) estimator for the linear correlated random coefficients (CRC) model. The CRC model is a natural generalization of the standard linear IV model that allows for endogenous, multivalued treatments and unobserved heterogeneity in treatment effects. The estimator implemented by ivcrc uses recent semiparametric identification results that allow for flexible functional forms and permit instruments that may be binary, discrete, or continuous. The ivcrc module also allows for the estimation of varying coefficients regressions, which are closely related in structure to the proposed IV estimator. We illustrate use of ivcrc by estimating the returns to education in the National Longitudinal Survey of Young Men.
